hints.title: Sorting Overhead Obstacle
hints.text: Following a cell's arrow is free and changing it costs one, so every move costs either 0 or 1. Is there a cheaper way to order the exploration than a general shortest-path method?

hints.title: Double-Ended Queue Ordering
hints.text: Use a double-ended queue to keep frontier states sorted by cumulative cost in linear time. Zero-cost movements along the existing arrow are placed at the front, while one-cost modifications are placed at the back.

hints.title: Frontier Expansion and Early Return
hints.text: Initialize a distance matrix with infinity and set dist[0][0] = 0. Push (0, 0, 0) to a deque. While the deque is not empty, pop the front state. If it reaches the bottom-right cell, return its cost. For each of the four directions, if moving there matches the grid arrow the weight is 0, else 1. If the new cost improves the neighbor distance, record it and push weight-0 moves to the front and weight-1 moves to the back.

hints.title: Complete Implementation

complexity.notes: 0-1 BFS using deque with push-front for weight 0 and push-back for weight 1.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Standard Dijkstra uses a binary heap with O(log(M * N)) operations per extraction, yielding O(M * N log(M * N)) time. Because edge weights are restricted strictly to {0, 1}, heap-based sorting adds unnecessary overhead compared to direct deque queueing.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Using an O(M * N) double-ended queue (deque) maintains monotonically non-decreasing distances without sorting by pushing weight-0 transitions to the front and weight-1 transitions to the back, achieving optimal O(M * N) linear time.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Explaining why 0-1 BFS maintains the monotonic priority queue invariant without a heap; pruning non-optimal paths with cost > dist[r][c]; mapping the 1-indexed directions 1=right, 2=left, 3=lower, 4=upper accurately.
